method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0' (Version 8.0, June 2024). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at the Creative Commons Licence statement on page 2 of https://www.cdc.gov.au/system/files/2025-09/coronavirus-covid-19-cdna-national-guidelines-for-public-health-units.pdf). Based on Commonwealth of Australia (interim Australian Centre for Disease Control) material, used under CC BY 4.0; claims are summarised in our words with the source passages quoted unchanged.

claims.claim: **Infectious period:** from 48 hours before symptoms (or a positive test if asymptomatic) until acute symptoms settle, which may take up to 10 days; a few people, and those with severe disease or marked immunocompromise, stay infectious longer.
claims.source_text: The start of the infectious period for COVID-19 is considered to be from 48 hours prior to symptom onset (or positive test if asymptomatic) (37). In general, individuals may be considered infectious until they are free of acute symptoms, which may be up to 10 days (37). Only a very small proportion of people may remain infectious for longer than this (38). People who are asymptomatic may still shed virus and infect others over this period (39-41). Individuals with severe disease, or who are significantly immunocompromised may be infectious for longer periods (42).
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A positive NAAT or RAT does not prove someone is still infectious** — both can detect non-viable viral shedding.
claims.source_text: Testing, with either a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) or rapid antigen test (RAT) cannot reliably determine infectivity as these tests can detect non-viable viral shedding that does not necessarily correlate with infectivity
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Incubation has shortened with each variant:** 5 to 7 days (median) for ancestral strains, and a pooled mean of 3.5 days (BA.1) to 4.1 days (BA.2) for Omicron.
claims.source_text: The median incubation period of ancestral strains of SARS-CoV-2 is 5 to 7 days, with a range of 1 to 14 days (28-30). However, successively shorter incubation periods have been identified for each emerging VOC (31-35). Current estimates for the pooled mean incubation period for different sublineages of Omicron range from 3.5 days for BA.1, to 4.1 days for BA.2 (36).
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Symptoms overlap with other respiratory infections** (fever, sore throat, cough, breathlessness, loss of smell or taste, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms); COVID-19 cannot be told apart without a test.
claims.source_text: COVID-19 presents with similar symptoms to other acute respiratory infections (ARI), such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Symptoms may include: • fever • chills • sore throat • sneezing • shortness of breath • runny nose • cough • loss of smell and/or taste • headache • fatigue • muscle or body aches • nausea (with or without vomiting) • diarrhoea. COVID-19 cannot be distinguished from other respiratory viral illnesses without diagnostic testing.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Age is the strongest risk factor, especially over 70 years.** Chronic illness, immunocompromise, Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people, residential care, disability and pregnancy also raise the risk; vaccination substantially lowers it.
claims.source_text: Older age is strongly associated with increased risk of severe disease and death, with risk significantly greater for those older than 70 years of age compared with younger people (59-62). People who have existing chronic health conditions, are immunocompromised, are Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people, live in residential care facilities, are living with a disability, or are pregnant, may also be at increased risk of severe disease and death (63, 64). Vaccination significantly reduces the risk of severe disease and death in at-risk groups (65-69).
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **People at increased risk should agree a COVID-19 plan with their GP in advance,** to act on if they develop respiratory symptoms or test positive.
claims.source_text: Persons at increased risk of severe disease should be encouraged to discuss with their general practitioner the development of a COVID-19 plan for implementation if they develop ARI or test positive for COVID-19.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Vaccination remains the most important protection against severe outcomes,** though it does little to stop infection or spread. A primary course is recommended for everyone 18 and over, and for children from 6 months at increased risk; further doses every 6–12 months for some groups.
claims.source_text: Vaccination remains the most important measure to protect against severe outcomes from COVID-19. Vaccines for SARS-CoV-2 are very effective at minimising the risk of severe disease and death but have limited effectiveness in preventing infection or transmission of the virus to others. The Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation recommends a primary course of COVID-19 vaccination for all Australians aged 18 years and over. A primary course is recommended for children aged 6 months to less than 18 years at increased risk of severe disease or death from COVID-19. Further COVID-19 vaccinations are recommended every 6-12 months for certain groups based on age and risk factors for severe disease.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Test early if at increased risk and symptomatic** — early testing opens access to oral antiviral treatment for eligible people.
claims.source_text: Emphasise the importance of early testing for people who are at increased risk of severe disease who have symptoms compatible with COVID-19. Early testing enables steps to be taken to limit onward transmission and facilitate access to oral antiviral treatments for eligible people.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **People at increased risk with acute respiratory symptoms should seek medical advice promptly;** early use of appropriate antivirals can prevent severe infection.
claims.source_text: proactively seek prompt medical advice to consider the need for testing for SARS-CoV-2 (and other respiratory pathogens) if at increased risk of severe disease. Early use of appropriate antiviral medications can prevent severe infection.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Clinical care is the treating clinician's job, not the public health unit's;** high-risk cases should be encouraged to seek medical care early.
claims.source_text: PHUs are not routinely involved in individual clinical management of COVID-19 cases. The medical management of individual cases is the responsibility of the case's healthcare provider. … Recommend seeking early medical care for cases at increased risk of severe disease or in high-risk settings.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **NAAT (e.g. PCR) is the diagnostic gold standard;** a RAT is a faster, more accessible alternative but less sensitive, so false negatives are more common.
claims.source_text: The gold standard for diagnosing acute symptomatic COVID-19 infection is with a NAAT (e.g., reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction). RATs may be used as an alternative and more accessible testing method, providing fast results following the correct collection of an appropriate respiratory sample. RATs have been approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration for home or point-of-care use to detect the presence of viral protein from SARS-CoV-2. RAT sensitivity is inherently lower than that of NAATs, resulting in a higher rate of false negative tests.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No drug is approved in Australia for pre- or post-exposure prophylaxis.**
claims.source_text: However, there are presently no pharmaceutical agents approved for use in Australia for this purpose.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cases should stay home until acute symptoms resolve (usually 5 to 7 days);** they can infect others for up to 10 days after symptom onset.
claims.source_text: Information for cases should advise they have the potential to infect others for up to 10 days after the onset of symptoms, with a very small proportion of people infectious for longer than this (38). Cases should be strongly advised to stay at home until their acute symptoms have resolved (usually 5 to 7 days).
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **While symptomatic:** wear a mask indoors on necessary trips out, work or study from home where possible, keep up hand and respiratory hygiene, avoid crowds and follow workplace policies.
claims.source_text: wear a mask when indoors for necessary trips outside the home • work or study from home where feasible • undertake appropriate hand and respiratory hygiene • avoid crowded areas • observe local work health and safety policies.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Highly immunocompromised people can stay infectious for a long time;** their treating physician should guide how long they stay home.
claims.source_text: Persons who are highly immunocompromised can be infectious for prolonged periods. These cases should be guided by their treating physician on the length of time they should stay at home and employ additional mitigations when outside the home (81).
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Contact tracing is not routine.** Asymptomatic contacts should watch for symptoms, keep up hygiene and follow workplace advice.
claims.source_text: Contact tracing for COVID-19 cases is not routinely undertaken in Australia. … Asymptomatic contacts of a COVID-19 case should: • monitor for symptoms and if symptoms develop, manage as per recommendations for people with acute respiratory symptoms • practice correct hand and respiratory hygiene • follow workplace advice.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Keep cases away from aged care and hospitals** until acute symptoms have resolved **and** at least 7 days have passed since onset (or since a positive test if asymptomatic); follow local timeframes.
claims.source_text: Clearly advise people with COVID-19 or symptoms of ARI, through appropriately tailored public messaging, not to visit settings where there are people at high risk of severe disease (e.g. residential aged care homes (RACH), or hospitals) until both acute symptoms have resolved and at least 7 days from symptom onset (or 7 days after testing positive if asymptomatic).
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Household contacts should put off visiting high-risk settings for at least 7 days after last contact;** if a visit is unavoidable, wear a surgical mask and keep distance.
claims.source_text: Advise asymptomatic household and household-like contacts of COVID-19 cases to defer visits to high-risk settings until at least 7 days have passed since their last contact with a COVID-19 case, other than for necessary reasons such as seeking medical attention. If a visit to a high-risk setting cannot be avoided, advise contacts to wear a surgical face mask and observe physical distancing.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Public health response times:** a new variant of concern within 24 hours; outbreaks in high-risk settings within one working day; other cases are routine.
claims.source_text: Respond immediately, within 24 hours, where there is a new VOC whose characteristics require the need for urgent public health action. Act as soon as possible, generally within one working day, for outbreaks in high-risk settings. All other COVID-19 cases may be considered routine.
claims.locator: Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) / interim Australian Centre for Disease Control, 'Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units, Version 8.0', Version 8.0, June 2024, https://www.cdc.gov.au/resources/publications/cdna-national-guidelines-covid-19, retrieved 2026-09-23
